The research group finds some interesting data coming from one of the potential planets they sent probes to.
He finds his girlfriend was taken by a military group because she was involved with the war somehow.
The team finds that there is intelligent life elsewhere in the galaxy but they’re on their infancy.
She is murdered. War erupts.
The team is going to escape. They too are targets for the opposing side because they’re intellectuals and thus dangerous to the new regime.
They give him the data from the probe asking him to keep it secret.
He flees to another country and publishes an article revealing the location of a solar system rich in some mineral needed by humans and suggests that there is NO signs of intelligent life on the galaxy and we should stop looking because that’s a waste of resources. We are alone.
His text becomes incredibly trascendental but without his girlfriend he doesn’t really care for anything anymore. Disappointed of humanity he retreats somewhere over the mountains.
A detective finds some unusual activity going around the moon city.
Software engineers are disappearing left and right.
The events coincide with the disappearance of a probe sent to a distant solar system to find minable planets.
A new religion is gaining traction. The detective suspects they are behind the unusual activity.
He finds that the religion is a suicide cult of people who want to transcend this reality.
The detective confronts the head of the religion who happens to be the author of the famous We are alone text.
They reveal their purpose of creating life (G A.I.) and kill themselves on the spot.
Millions of people across several planets commit suicide.
The detective is sad.
The greatest assassin in the galaxy  is foolishly spotted during a mission on planet earth. She tried to locate the witness but fails.
She thinks of herself as an agent of entropy and only kills those she deems contributors of evil to the universe. She wants to maximize the amount of happiness in it. For this she happens to have an special ability.
A writer had struggled with getting published for the longest time until one day he daydreams a fantastic story. He doesn’t know where the story came from but he manages to publish it in a well respected magazine. It becomes rather popular and they aske him to write some more.
The witness contacts the assassin and reveals he wants to hire her services to stop a thief.
The writer duels on the fact that he doesn’t know how to get the inspiration again. He is attacked by a gang one day and a man in a suit suggests him to stop writing that kind of stories because it doesn’t match the views of the Martian society. [Connect with the revolution maybe?]
The assassin follows and investigates her target who turns out to be the writer. Wondering why the witness want him dead or why he thinks he fits her criteria she decides to postpone the kill.
She turns to investigate the witness instead. The assassin discovers the true identity of the witness: the detective.
The writer delivers a new story for the magazine, this time written in a different style. His usual uninspired style. They turn down his proposal asking him to serialize his previous stories instead. He then tries to activate his daydream again.
This is how the assassin and the writer cross paths for the first time. She can’t kill him because he is contributing greatly to the universe’s entropy.
They confront the ai. They take their own decisions. Humanity is ready.

Ideas/Project-First-Born/T3---New-Struct.content:
T3 - New Structure

Chapter 1 | Daniel and the dawn The Human Destiny.
Same as before.
Daniel had been away for only a few days, but as he walked into his apartment, he could feel that everything had changed. The silence that greeted him was deafening and only exacerbated by the distant sirens of the planes flying above. The emptiness was palpable, as if the very air inside the apartment had been sucked out. He could sense her absence in every corner, every room, every inch of the space they had shared. He knew, with a sinking feeling in his gut, that she was gone.
He desperately searched for any sign that she had left, but all he found were her empty shoes and her watch still ticking away on the nightstand.
He looked at the file on his desk and remembered the day he was called in to work at AEM. He had been so excited. The letter had arrived in the morning bearing the seal of the space agency. It was a summons, and to Daniel it meant a new life, a new destiny.
Chapter 2 | The writer and his obsession with the dream world.
A writer who seeks for inspiration looking at the stars. One day he comes across a patch in the sky that seems rather empty. He starts looking for answers on this patch of darkness and comes across a paper written by Daniel, where he outlines how their team had reached the conclusion we are alone in the universe and pondered about our role in shaping it. This experience triggers a psychological collapse in the writer, who develops a sense of dread whenever he looks up to the night sky. Along with the phobia, he starts having dreams about humanity’s evolution. Here he sees humans from a God-like perspective and with time he becomes attached to some of  them, but is in fact powerless to help them. So he decides to keep their memories alive by writing about them. And that’s how he comes up with the stories in his books.
David Rothman had always looked to the stars, searching for the light of inspiration despite knowing there was nobody out there. He usually found comfort in their presence, like they were distant friends. However, on this particular night he found nothing but darkness.
Chapter 3 | The three proposals for human expansion and the violent death of the most promising mind.
In the future, humans have predicted the planet will die within 100 years due to a cosmic catastrophe. In response the governments of the world have united to develop a series of plans that will ensure the survival of the human race. After a few years they narrow it down to 3 plans that they will execute in the span of the last century, in hopes that at least one of them will succeed.
The clock was ticking, and the fate of humanity hung in the balance as the leaders of the world gathered for the first conference of the Survival Initiative. They had been given one century to save humanity from certain doom, and today, they would reveal the projects that would determine the fate of the human race. It was a desperate gamble, with three possible paths to salvation. The room was filled with tension. It was a momentous day, one that would decide the future of humanity and their legacy.
The details of each proposal were discussed with extreme caution and deliberation, their feasibility analyzed, and the resources allocated. But there was one voice that was not heard in the room, the voice of a young detective.
Chapter 4 | The detective investigating the murder.
Right after the presentation of the last proposal at the Survival Initiative, that of Dr. H.S. Where he revealed his controversial plan to send a light vessel containing only a human DNA virus with the objective of finding a host on a habitable planet and forcing it to eventually evolve into what we now know as humans, the vessel would be immediately followed by a large ship at a speed of .01 percent the speed of light, containing tons of human knowledge and technology. Hoping that, by the time the second ship arrives, humans will be sufficiently evolved to be able to decipher and understand the contents of the ship. Dr. H.S.  was also about to reveal they have found evidence of intelligent life elsewhere on the galaxy, but just as he was about to say the words, he was murdered.
There had been suspicion of a rebellious organization attempting to sabotage the Survival Initiative project for a long time but they never thought life’s were in danger, much less those of the academics leading the research to save our species. Because of that suspicion detective Kira Novak was placed within the audience when the murder took place. She was a very clever woman. She desperately worked to uncover the facts surrounding Dr. H.S.’s murder, but the investigation was made harder by the political and economic implications the whole affair was causing.
“There’s one more thing,” Dr. H.S. had said, right before he died. The words still hung to Kira’s mind as she combed through the evidence with single-minded determination. It was already past midnight, she was now alone in her office but she kept reliving the moment over and over in her mind’s eye.
A black jacket, brown running shoes, and a peculiar string that hung from her waist. Who was the killer?  Kira felt like the answer was just within her reach, yet still, she could not understand the pieces of the puzzle.

Ideas/Project-First-Born/Un-argumento-in.title: Project First Born - Un argumento interesante
Ideas/Project-First-Born/Un-argumento-in.content:
Un argumento interesante
Piensa the fermi paradox.
La idea que el universo siendo tan grande como es deberíamos encontrar señales de vida en todos lados, dado que la existencia de vida no debería ser poco común. Y asumiendo que la vida inteligente siempre busca expandirse, la galaxia debería estar repleta de vida.
Ahora asumamos nuestra existencia como extraordinaria. Por diversos factores, es posible que sólo nosotros pudiéramos existir en este marco de tiempo. Quizá la vida no es poco común pero sí somos especiales en un factor: somos los primeros.
What would happen then?
In science fiction there’s always the notion of some ancient beings who were able to scatter around the universe but then died in a tornado*. Or came to claim earth one day all of a sudden, or who cared for us in the shadows during humanity’s childhood.
También vemos un encuentro con otra civilización relativamente en el mismo nivel tecnológico que nosotros como un tema recurrente. En donde nuestra decisión entre hostilidad y hospitalidad es igualmente definida por las acciones del otro.
Sin embargo, la historia de estos viejos seres en este momento me parece mucho más interesante que el primer contacto.
¿Quienes eran? ¿qué vivieron? ¿a dónde fueron? ¿por qué y cómo fue que tomaron tal o cual postura ante otras formas de vida? y ¿Cómo fue enfrentarse a la absoluta soledad del universo? What’s it like to be the pioneers on this bitter sweet journey through the universe?
Por ello propongo desarrollar esta historia. La humanidad como la primera forma de vida en un universo vivo. Explorar, como en Aniara, los efectos de enfrentar nuestra soledad pero con la ambición de expansión siempre presente y la posibilidad de ser el villano en la historia de otra civilización emergente. Incluir, como en Foundation, estudios sociológicos de la humanidad como una masa predecible. Responder lo que significa ser humano y si la maldad nos es inherente.
*A typhon

Ideas/Puis-il--y-a-les-Faux-Souvenirs.content:
Elle portait un cardigan jaune pastel, une chemise blanche et une jupe noire à fleurs.
Nous nous sommes rencontrés dans une quincaillerie où elle travaillait à temps partiel. Je l’ai reconnue immédiatement. Tout à coup je suis retombé amoureux, et plus rien n’avait d’importance.
Il n’y avait que nous, ce moment, et toutes nos souvenirs, même lointains, qui nous liaient.
Elle était en train de déménager chez son copain. J’ai essayé de la convaincre de le quitter et de fuir avec moi à la place.
En me réveillant, je pensais encore à elle.
La matinée était passée comme d’habitude. J’ai fait du café, mangé un morceau, dit au revoir a ma copine et suis sorti pour aller au travail. Sauf que je ne suis pas allé au travaille. En fait j’ai marché jusqu’à la quincaillerie. Un homme barbu m’a salué.
Plus le temps passait, plus ma memoire s’évanouissait. Et le peur de la perdre encore me possédait. Son visage me semblait déjà distante. Mais encore le souvenir de son parfum restait, et soudain, une adresse m’est revenue à l’esprit. Celle de son copain chez qui elle voulait déménager.

Ideas/The-Hidden-Writer.title: The Hidden Writer
Ideas/The-Hidden-Writer.content:
Idea transcription:
There is a woman who teaches at a local high school, though she does not think of herself as a teacher first. Before anything else, she is a writer, or at least someone who once believed she would become one. Teaching is what happened when writing did not become a life, or not enough of one to live on. The subject she teaches may or may not matter. What matters is that the school is a high school, and that every day she stands in front of people at an age when everything still feels possible, while privately suspecting that possibility has long since passed her by.
She is lonely, or depressed, or simply tired in a way she has never learned to name. She has trouble connecting with people, not because she lacks feeling, but because feeling rarely seems to translate into anything useful. Even when things are good, she cannot seem to be happy in the expected way. With her girlfriend, perhaps, she was the happiest she had been in years, but even that happiness was muted, incomplete, not enough for her girlfriend and not enough for her. Then her girlfriend becomes convinced she has cheated on her. She has not, but the argument happens anyway, and they break up. The problem is that her girlfriend lives nearby — not next door, but close enough that she might run into her on the street, at the corner store, on the way back from work. After the breakup, the idea of seeing her becomes unbearable. She does not want her ex-girlfriend to see her doing well or doing badly. She does not want to offer her evidence of any kind. She does not want to exist for her as a changing, visible person anymore. It seems better that she become only an idea in her ex-girlfriend’s mind, something unresolved, something she cannot update.
So the next day after school she stalls. She stays in her classroom grading papers, or pretending to grade them, long past the hour when she could reasonably leave. She is not exactly planning anything at first. She is only delaying the moment when she has to go home. The school usually closes around seven, but that evening the caretaker or security guard assumes the building is empty and locks up a little early. The teacher realizes she has been left inside.
She does not panic. If anything, she feels relieved.
The school is large enough that she can avoid being noticed. There are multiple connected buildings, long hallways, dead corridors, stairwells that seem to lead nowhere important. She keeps quiet while the last noises of the evening fade away. Once she is sure she is alone except for the guard, she wanders. At first there is nothing especially mysterious about the place. It is only a school after hours: lockers, classrooms, bulletin boards, the stale smell of floor cleaner and paper. Eventually she returns to her classroom and spends the night there, writing in a notebook, doing nothing, letting time pass. In the morning, she acts as if she has arrived early.
But by the end of the next day, she again cannot bring herself to go home.
This time, she makes a choice. She hides in a small supply closet in the teachers’ lounge, one meant for coffee, sugar, paper towels, and other things no one checks carefully. She waits there until the school closes. After that, she slips out and takes possession of the night. She does this again the next day, and then again. For a few days, then perhaps for weeks, she stops going home. During the day she buys food, toiletries, small supplies — just enough to survive without drawing attention. At night she lives inside the school like a ghost.
At first it feels almost fun. Secret, childish, forbidden. The school becomes less like a workplace and more like a country she has discovered by accident. Her ordinary life has collapsed, but in this strange suspended version of living, she can breathe. She begins to write again. She tries one story, abandons it, starts another, abandons that too. Characters appear and dissolve. Plots begin with force and then go thin. The excitement of hiding gives her energy for a while, but not purpose.
Then she begins exploring more seriously. She searches for forgotten rooms, locked doors, obsolete hallways, places no one has reason to enter anymore. Eventually, deep inside the school, she finds an old storage room. It is not exactly a secret chamber, but it feels like one. It is full of discarded furniture: old desks, old chairs, test archives from years no one remembers, institutional things that have survived their usefulness. It has the feeling of a place erased without being removed.
And there, buried among everything else, she finds a typewriter.
Not just any typewriter. The model matters. It is one she wanted as a child, back when wanting to be a writer was still simple and bright. Maybe she once saw the same model in a shop when one of her parents took her there. Maybe it belonged to her father, who used one for work, and as a child she imagined inheriting the tool and transforming it into something artistic, something her own. The exact memory can remain uncertain. What matters is that the machine reaches her across time. It makes writing feel possible again, not abstractly, but physically. Keys, ink, paper, sound.
The room is so far removed from the rest of the building that no one can hear the clacking at night. She begins returning there after hours, typing with a seriousness she has not felt in years. For the first time in a long while, she feels close to making something.
Then there is a student.
The student is one of those kids who seems slightly out of step with everyone else. Not friendless, exactly, but often misunderstood. They speak too intensely about certain subjects — a show they love, a hobby, a world they carry inside themselves. They have friends, but the friendships seem conditional, scheduled, fragile: main friends, backup friends, people available between extracurriculars while waiting to be picked up. One afternoon, the student is left waiting at school too long. Their mother, or parent, says they will come, then later cancels and tells them to take the bus. The student has not really done that before, or at least not from there, not alone. Maybe they have forgotten their keys and cannot get inside the house until someone returns. Maybe it is not dangerous, only inconvenient, but the teacher cannot quite leave them standing there.
She talks to them first out of pity, or concern, or because she recognizes something. She asks if everything is all right. The conversation continues. She offers to help them get home, or to wait with them, or to take them somewhere to eat while they kill time. They end up at McDonald’s, or some other ordinary place made meaningful only because they sit there too long and talk more honestly than either of them expected.
Afterward, they walk through the city. Perhaps the city is plain, forgettable, nothing like Paris, so they pretend that it is Paris. They look at the river and call it the Seine. They cross a bridge and imagine it belongs to another life. They make a game of seeing their own boring streets through the eyes of tourists, marveling at the way light falls on ugly buildings, how a dirty railing can become beautiful if described with enough conviction. For a little while, the pretending works.
Then the conversation turns darker, or deeper. They talk about why people go on. What motives are enough. Whether things get better or whether people only learn to continue. The teacher, for reasons she may not understand, answers honestly. Too honestly, perhaps. She says she does not really know why she wakes up every day. She says she has been on autopilot since she was nineteen, or since graduation, or since some unnamed point when life stopped feeling like it was beginning and started feeling like maintenance. She does not say this cruelly. She does not intend to hurt the student. She may even think there is comfort in admitting uncertainty. But there are truths that adults should not hand to children without also offering a way back from them, and she may fail to do that.
They part ways. The student goes home. For the first time in weeks, so does she.
Her apartment feels alien. Everything is exactly as she left it. Nothing has spoiled because there was barely anything there to spoil. She realizes she was living day to day long before she started sleeping at school. Her secret life has not disrupted a healthy routine; it has only made visible the absence that was already there. She cleans a little. Straightens things. Packs a small bag with books she has been meaning to read, books that might feed the story, notebooks, maybe clothes, maybe whatever else she needs to return to the school and stay hidden a little longer. Just long enough to finish the novel, she tells herself. After that she can go back to life. Turn herself around. Become someone again.
But when she returns to school, the student is absent.
At first this means nothing. Students miss school. They get sick. Families travel. Parents make decisions. Children transfer. People disappear from a classroom for entirely ordinary reasons. But because the teacher has their conversation in her mind, she begins to treat the absence as evidence. She replays the walk, the bridge, the invented Paris, the things she said and the things she did not say. She begins to find clues in retrospect, as though guilt has given her a new form of intelligence. She becomes afraid the student has killed themselves.
No one at the school mentions anything. There is no announcement, no solemn meeting, no whisper that reaches her. This should reassure her, but it does not. The silence becomes part of the terror. It is possible nothing happened. It is possible the student simply has the flu, or changed schools, or stayed home for a week. It is also possible that the school knows and is saying nothing, or that she has missed the signs, or that the student was never as real as they seemed. The reader does not have to know. She does not know either.
She goes back to the storage room and writes. Without meaning to, she creates a character who resembles the student. Not exactly, not in a way anyone else might prove, but enough that she recognizes it. The character has the same intensity, the same loneliness, the same way of turning ordinary things into private worlds. At first the teacher tells herself it is accidental. Writers borrow from life. That is what writing is. But after a few pages, or a few days, she can no longer deny that the character is the student, or the student as she fears them to be.
And in the story, the character has to die.
She does not know whether she is predicting, confessing, punishing herself, or trying to control something unknowable by turning it into fiction. When she writes the death, it feels less like invention than participation. She feels as if she has done it herself — not with her hands, but with her failure to be someone better. If the student is dead, then she should have noticed. She should not have spoken so bleakly. She should have known that honesty without hope can be a kind of abandonment. If the student is alive, then her guilt is irrational, but that does not save her from it.
The novel becomes the place where every failure gathers: the failed writer, the failed teacher, the failed lover, the failed adult on the bridge who could not offer a child a reason to continue because she did not have one for herself. She thinks of her ex-girlfriend and how even her happiness had not looked like happiness. She thinks of the apartment, the school, the storage room, the typewriter, the way hiding had briefly felt like freedom. She thinks of the student, absent or imagined or dead or simply elsewhere.
Eventually, she goes back to the bridge.
Whether she brings the manuscript with her is uncertain. Maybe she leaves it in her classroom where someone will find it, because some part of her still wants to be read. But that feels almost too hopeful. More likely, she leaves it in the hidden storage room beside the typewriter, signed but not presented, finished or unfinished, proud of it and ashamed of needing pride. She does not believe the work matters enough to save her. If she did, perhaps she would stay and try to publish it. So she leaves it where no one goes, in the one place that made her feel like a writer again.
Then she disappears into the river, or into the idea of the river, and does not return.
Afterward, no one finds the manuscript. Or maybe someone does years later. The student may return to school after a week away and hear what happened to the teacher. If so, they may understand too much. They may remember the bridge, the false Paris, the conversation about going on, and feel the same useless guilt she felt for them. Or perhaps they never return. Or perhaps they were never in danger at all. Perhaps the teacher built an entire tragedy around an absence that had a simple explanation.
The story does not have to answer that. Its center is not the fact of what happened to the student, but the space created by not knowing — the way loneliness turns uncertainty into proof, the way a writer can mistake imagination for truth, the way a person can vanish from life while still showing up every day, until even the places meant to hold children and noise and routine become a refuge for someone who no longer knows how to go home.

Ideas/Un-petit-homme.title: Idea - Un petit homme
Ideas/Un-petit-homme.content:
Il y avait un fois un homme tout simple qui vivait une vie toute simple. 
Chaque matin il se levait, prenait le petit-déjeuner et se mettait à travailler jusqu’à la nuit. Personne ne savait exactement ce qu’il faisait, mais il n’avait jamais vis une journée sans travailler.
Il n’y avait rien de spécial à propos de lui sauf le fait qu’il ne pouvait pas tomber amoureux. En fait, il ne pouvait pas se donner a aucune sentiment très puissant car il était petit. Il était tellement petit. Aussi petit qu’un stylo.

Ideas/Untitled-Space-Story.title: Untitled Space Story
Ideas/Untitled-Space-Story.content:
Untitled
En los puertos del norte tenían un nombre para los transportistas estacionados en el ártico: “Carburantes”. Principalmente debido a su cercanía a los antiguos motores que se alimentan de combustibles fósiles. Era un término que a Ael siempre le había molestado, le parecía ofensivo que los asociaran con el olor de sus motores y no con el calor que emanaban. Por eso cuando el ex-comandante Ludvig se refirió a ella como transportista, decidió confiar en él. Era un personaje peculiar. Era alto, corpulento, y con una miríada de cicatrices que contaban la triste historia de su vida. Pero Ael no se dejaba llevar por las apariencias y aunque la persona que tenía frente a ella poseía un aura imponente, ahora se arrodillaba ante ella como un cachorro indefenso.
— Si decides negarte yo lo entenderé. no deberás preocuparte por agentes Planetarios y podrás seguir comerciando. Pero te ruego que al menos consideres mi oferta.
— A mí no me parece una oferta muy lucrativa. No me interesa lo que esté en juego para ti, no pienso cruzar el ecuador por nada menos que el doble de la tarifa establecida y si mi nave queda hecha pedazos te juro que te encontraré aunque te escondas en los confines del mundo.
— No te preocupes, el cargamento es seguro.
— Eso dices, pero yo jamás he escuchado de alguien transportando 35 toneladas de diamante desde un polo helado. Además, alguien en tu posición debería tener contactos para mover este cargamento dentro de la atmósfera.
— Me halaga que aún guardes ese concepto de mí, pero el imperio me dio la espalda hace muchos años. En lo que a ellos concierne mi cuerpo yace aún congelado en Europa.
— Es un riesgo extra entregar mercancía de un hombre muerto.
Ael se levantó de su asiento y se dirigió a la salida y el silencio que la precedía parecía hacer la negociación por ella.
— ¿Qué te parece esto? Pagaré el precio que pidas y además, al terminar el trato, podrás quedarte con la mercancía. Sólo asegúrate que revisen la legitimidad de todo el cargamento.
Se detuvo a unos pasos de la salida y volteó buscando los ojos de aquel hombre.
— ¿Las 35 toneladas?
— Todo menos un diamante. Por un momento los ojos del ex-comandante Ludvig revelaron una sagacidad perturbadora y en ese instante se desvanecieron todas las dudas que la rodeaban. Ael sonrió sin darse cuenta.
— De acuerdo, tú ganas.
__
La habitación principal del palacio parecía pertenecer a un época distinta, mientras que la frugalidad determinaba el estilo del resto del edificio, la habitación de la emperatriz estaba repleta de adornos, en las paredes, poseía techos increíblemente altos y un ventanal que enmarcaba la ciudad entera. Por las tardes el sol inundaba el lugar y rebotaba sobre los detalles de oro. Sin embargo ahora estaba en penumbra y parecía un lugar distinto. Sobre la mesa una taza de té se enfriaba. Maya, en un sillón junto a una de las gigantescas ventanas, contaba los minutos de silencio que le quedaban mientras observaba la ciudad que dormía a sus pies. Nadie dentro de su gabinete era capaz de entender el origen de su intermitente insomnio. Como gobernante de la próspera ciudad capital era adulada, como emperatriz del planeta era respetada, y como la responsable de mantener el asedio perpetuo de la ciudad invisible era temida y odiada. 
Maya no era la primera gobernante en encontrar resistencia por parte de sus habitantes, pero sí la primera que se enfrentó a una fuerza superior para mantener el secreto de la existencia de la ciudad. 
Su piel, ahora pálida y sin brillo, comenzaba a proyectar la imagen de una emperatriz enferma. Pero esto poco le preocupaba. Serían los historiadores quienes decidirían la forma de su legado, y estaba convencida que serían benévolos. Mientras, ella debía concentrarse en un objetivo: Mantener el secreto de la ciudad invisible y enfrentar la única crisis que ninguno de sus predecesores había encontrado; Tara, la telépata de la ciudad invisible que había logrado unificar los distintos sindicatos de la ciudad. 
Bajo la organización de la telépata, los ciudadanos habían logrado violar el asedio en más de una ocasión. Pero lo peor había sido la irreverencia de Tara ante el imperio y esta noche su nombre de nuevo acechaba su sueño. Un mensaje desde la ciudad invisible venía en camino, envuelto en misterio, transportado entre las sombras. A pesar del retraso, Maya ya sabía quién era el remitente; aquella que acechaba sus pensamientos, quien le había hurtado palabras de sus labios sellados y que ahora quería hablar.
Maya acarició la suave superficie del descansabrazos de su sillón y la puerta del otro lado del inmenso salón se disolvió en un instante. 
Aro, su mano derecha, la única persona que tenía permitido el acceso a esa habitación, atravesó la sala en silencio, siguiendo el camino marcado por la alfombra roja. Se acercó y sacó de su abrigo un pequeño sobre que entregó solemnemente. Maya lo observó con detenimiento, notó que estaba tibio, y era ligeramente pesado.
— ¿Esto es todo?
— Dentro del sobre hay dos objetos. El mensajero solicitó que sólo usted viera el contenido, aunque nos tomamos la molestia de analizarlo para asegurar su seguridad.
— ¿Quién más sabe de esto?
— En este momento usted y yo somos los únicos vivos al tanto del paquete.
Al extender el contenido del sobre sobre el escritorio, lo primero que llamó la atención de Maya fue el papel en el que estaba escrita la carta. La tinta sobre el punto final manchó su pulgar.
Aro permanecía estoico por lo que Maya tuvo dificultades para descifrar lo que sentía.
— El té se ha enfriado. Las palabras parecieron flotar en aquella fría habitación, el eco retumbaba en las paredes como hielo resquebrajándose.
Aro tomó la taza, y salió de la sala.
No parecía el clásico papel infinitamente reciclado que ella asociaba con la ciudad invisible. El mero uso de un bien importado le parecía un mensaje de insubordinación.
Leyó la carta en silencio. Un cargamento extraviado ahora pedía acceso desde el norte. Deslizaba velozmente la mirada por la página, apenas registrando las palabras hasta que algo captó su atención: “Que tu legado sea uno de compasión. Permite que nosotros seamos la voz de tu recuerdo.”
La presencia de Aro regresó su mente al presente. Su sigilo era respetuoso. Colocó el té sobre la mesa y se dio media vuelta pero, antes de poder retirarse Maya lo detuvo levantando el brazo.
— Espera. Quiero tu opinion. ¿Puedes probarlo?
Un pequeño sorbo fue suficiente.
— ¿Cómo crees que lo hizo?
— ¿Enviar la carta?
— ¿Cómo logró colarse en mi mente? Fui cuidadosa, he seguido las sugerencias de todas las posibles religiones y supersticiones. Pero no importa lo que haga ella siempre sabe lo que estoy pensando. Siempre se coloca un paso frente a mi.
— Yo no creo que sea verdaderamente una telépata. Deben tener métodos nefastos para infiltrarse y difundir información sin que el imperio pueda impedirlo.
— Por supuesto que no es telepatía. Pero he hecho todo. Cerré toda posible vía de comunicación, cada onda electromagnética es vigilada, el espacio aéreo ha estado cerrado por más de 50 años, todo vínculo fuera de la atmósfera fuera cercenado. Y aún así.
Hubo un incomodo silencio que crecía con cada segundo, separándolos cada vez más. La respiración de Aro era cada vez más agitada. Maya lo observaba esperando aún una respuesta.
— Quizás la voluntad de generaciones se ha estado filtrando entre las grietas de los muros. Su deseo de formar parte de algo más grande que su ciudad.
— Ya forman parte de la única fuente inagotable de energía. Están ayudando a todo el sistema a sobrevivir. ¿Acaso no es suficiente?
— Alimentando a su vez una guerrera eterna, Aro interpuso. Sus palabras escaparon de su boca sin pensarlo pero la reacción de la emperatriz lo había sorprendido aún más.
— La guerra más necesaria en la historia de la humanidad. Quizás la única justificada, y la única que se ha mantenido con los mismos soldados desde hace un siglo.
— ¿A cambio de qué? preguntó de pronto. Aro ya no podía contener sus ideas. Aquellos soldados han resucitado tantas veces que perdieron su humanidad. El suero que produce la ciudad invisible hace tiempo que dejó de ser un milagro.
— Sin embargo viven y el imperio prospera.
Aro llevó su mano al pecho, parecía perder más fuerza con cada respiración. Fragmentos de su vida arrancados violentamente de sus pulmones. La lucha de su pecho sonaba como un tambor, con un ritmo cada vez más acelerado. Sus ojos, inflamados de rabia y lágrimas buscaban condenar a alguien, pero las palabras ya no lograban salir de su boca. Su colapso fue silencioso, como lo había sido su vida.
— No pretendan ser ustedes quienes llevarán mi recuerdo al futuro. Ahora, sí me permites. Tengo una nave que interceptar, dijo Maya.
A través de la ventana el sol comenzaba a asomarse. Una noche más sin dormir. ¿Cuánto más podría resistir?
__
Había una cualidad indescriptible en la atmósfera que incomodaba a Ael. No se trataba del aire o las condiciones meteorológicas que, aunque poco favorables no representaban un reto para un piloto experimentado; aquella era más bien una sospecha que continuaba creciendo en su alma por cada kilómetro recorrido.
Sobre el amplio océano del hemisferio sur el viaje era monótono, las nubes a su alrededor comenzaban a electrizarse cada vez más, y la visibilidad disminuía. Ael decidió establecer el curso automático y soltar el mando por un momento. Lo cierto es que la curiosidad que sentía era insoportable, las palabras del viejo retumbaban en su cabeza, perfectamente claras pero aún así su significado parecía indescifrable.
Se acercó a los contenedores con cautela, cuidando no dejar rastros de su incursión, y los abrió uno por uno para revisar los diamantes. Jamás le habían confiado un cargamento tan valioso. El tenue zumbido que producían al mantener la temperatura estable creaba un ambiente apacible dentro de la nave. Uno de los contenedores le llamó la atención, era más cálido al tacto, un cambio casi imperceptible pero ella lo notó y pensó por un momento que el viejo motor de su nave podía haberlo afectado. A pesar de ello, prefirió primero examinar los diamantes. Acercó un pequeño dispositivo a cada uno de los diamantes que emitía una leve cantidad de luz ultravioleta haciendo que los diamantes brillaran brevemente de un vivido azul cielo.
Le pareció por un momento que transportaba las estrellas y notó como dentro del contenedor, una de ellas titilaba. Era genuino pero cada vez que lo leía el resultado era igual. Una vacilación, una danza de luz, y después un resultado positivo.
Un trueno lejano resonó entre las nubes, profundo como una advertencia. La calma dentro de la nave se quebró apenas por un instante, y Ael alzó la vista. Afuera, los relámpagos creaban por instantes una red de luz sobre el oscuro océano, y las siluetas de cientos de naves se dejaron ver.
— Atención nave 6-7-M.I.M.E está entrando a una zona restringida. Cese toda propulsión inmediatamente e indique su destino.
Ninguno de los mapas abordo mostraban algún asentamiento en aquellas coordenadas, de eso estaba segura. Había revisado hasta los mapas impresos que nadie se había molestado en actualizar y consultó con sus compañeros en el ártico pero todos le aseguraron lo mismo: Ahí no encontrarás nada. Desde el principio le pareció extraño, una entrega en medio del océano. Pensó que se encontraría con otra nave, quizo creer que el trabajo realmente sería algo sencillo, le entregaría los diamantes y eso sería todo. Lo último que esperaba era ser recibida por la guardia imperial haciendo preguntas sobre su cargamento. Maldijo a Ludvig entre dientes, tendría que cobrarle extra cuando lo viera.
Retomó la calma y transmitió sus datos, y la información del cargamento con un tono sobrio. Todo parecía estar en orden. Sin embargo, las naves permanecían en su sitio. El silencio se la incomodaba. Llenó su nave sin que se diera cuenta y la acorraló.
— Nave 6-7-M.I.M.E será abordada para una inspección. Permanezca en su sitio.
Cuando entraron Ael ya se encontraba de rodillas y con las manos en la nuca.
Decenas de soldados inundaron su nave en un instante y comenzaron a inspeccionar sistemáticamente cada rincón en busca de algún acompañante pero ella estaba sola. Esa soledad que ella siempre había intentado ignorar jamás le había parecido tan presente, tan pesada.
No sintió miedo cuando le apuntaron con sus rifles, ni cuando le gritaron maldiciones y prometieron que la matarían si movía algún músculo. Pero el miedo comenzó a asentarse en su corazón cuando notaron su soledad.
— No hay nadie, dijo una voz desde lo más profundo de su nave. Y aquellos soldados se relajaron, tomaron sus armas como quien carga una sombrilla justo antes de la llovizna. Se reían. Ael mantenía la vista en el suelo pero sentía sus miradas y sabía que era la causa de sus risas. Uno de los soldados la pateó por la espalda haciéndola caer y descansó su bota sobre ella.
— No sabes ni donde te metiste.
Las palabras retumbaron en sus entrañas y el miedo crecía. Sus dedos temblaban y si se hubiese podido levantar, habrían visto sus ojos llenos de lágrimas.
Esta era la guardia de hielo, honrando su fama como el ejército inhumano que defendía a la emperatriz. Era bien sabido entre los transportistas que sí los encontrabas en tu camino, más te valía rendirte o asegurarte de que podrías huir.
Revisaron el cargamento minuciosamente. No lograron encontrar nada sospechoso o fuera de lugar. Sin embargo, no se iban. Aquella espera le pareció interminable a Ael. De pronto los soldados retomaron su actitud disciplinada, se colocaron firmes, en fila a lo largo de la entrada y levantaron los brazos en señal de saludo. Era como verlos convertirse en soldados de plástico.
Entonces la vió. Entró despreocupada y

Maya sospecha que Ael no sabe nada y que es imparcial. Quiere usarla. La arresta, la intenta convencer, la libera pero la siguen en secreto para encontrar a Tata.

Tara no es telépata sino que está trabajando junto con Ludvig y otros para tratar de mejorar la calidad de vida en la ciudad con ayuda del exterior y al mismo tiempo intentan liberar la ciudad.
Su método de comunicación son mensajes codificados dentro de diamantes alterados con “Asimetría temporal”.
El imperio mantiene una guerra perpetua en Europa usando soldados que revive con el suero que extrae en la ciudad invisible. La guerra se financia con los diamantes que extraen de Europa y al mismo tiempo son un ingrediente importante en la generación del suero.
Ludvig solía ser un comandante en Europa pero logró escapar su destino usando medios desconocidos.
Ael es imparcial pero decide tomar el lado de la ciudad invisible por principios. Logra escapar y ocultar el diamante importante gracias a su conocimiento de los motores de gasolina.

index.content:
Hello! I’m Emmanuel 👋
I have a background in filmmaking and I work as a video editor, so I’ve always been interested in storytelling, and in the impermanence and brevity of things. I often think of the traces that stay with us after things are gone. Like the dream that vanishes the moment you wake up, or the film whose final image stays in your mind long after it fades to black, or even the characters who keep asking questions in your mind after you’ve closed a book.
This is where I collect those traces as best I can.
